doc.title: Jimmy and Jeannie Cheatham interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 12, 1998

chapter: Papa Jo Jones and the Sweet Baby Blues Band
title: Sharing, family among musicians and Milt Hinton
summary: Duvivier, a Milt Hinton story about funerals, and Jimmy on the musician family and the need for an oasis; Jeannie's mother quotes 'The Whole World is a Ghetto'.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: Well he certainly was one of the important people in the line of drummers, wasn’t he?
Yeah.
And George Duvivier was another.
George Duvivier was another you see.
And in fact who was that, John Young? John Young is one of our friends here. He’s a musician who used to play at the Apollo Theater.
Former saxophone player.

But he’s a very good friend of Milt Hinton’s. And he called us up last week and he said Milt Hinton called him up and told him, “John, I went to a funeral of one of our friends last week.” And John said, “yeah?” He said yeah he was talking to the funeral director and everybody was getting ready to leave, and he said he told the funeral director, gee whiz, I’ve been out here too much this year. He said three or four of my friends have been laid to rest. And so the funeral director asked him, “Well how old were they?” “Well one was 70, one was 72, and one was 75.” So the funeral director says, “Well how old are you?” He says “I’m 89.” He said, “Well you might as well not go home, you might as well stay here.”
That cold, wasn’t it?
You don’t say that to Milt Hinton.
He said the man told him that.
He called up John Young, and John Young called us. I said oh please. And that’s the other thing about sharing.
Yeah sharing.

And that the way in terms of how we came up, with that whole — there was always family. You always, “Hey, how you feeling today, everything all right?” And if they weren’t together, wherever they were, they could be in Europe, and all of a sudden they’d get this thing about, well let me call Jim and Jeannie. Say hi, how y’all doing, blah, blah, blah, blah. Well I’ll be home so-and-so and so-and-so, but I was just thinking about you so I just wanted to let you know. And that’s the way it was, that whole connection. And that, to me, represents the oasis. And that’s what we need, is an oasis, not only for the musicians, but for the whole human race.
Jimmy — the whooole human— it’s true, we do need it.
Well I mean that’s how we’re all going to get in tune to this— one sun and one moon out here.

Because my mother, she’s a bit more pessimistic, she calls us, she listens to everything. She calls us up and she says, “Listen have you heard that song ‘The Whole World is a Ghetto’ by that group called War?”
That was pretty wild.
I said what? She says, “You know they’re right.”
Is this recent? Fairly recent?
That’s when they had that record. They had that hit on there.
Yeah. She listens to everything. She’s 89 now.
Yeah. She’s surprising, all the time.
